of 1,3-Enynes under an Air Atmosphere

ABSTRACT: A ball-mill-enabled nickel-catalyzed 1,4-alkylaryla-
tion of 1,3-enynes with organic bromides has been developed,
offering a versatile method for assembling tetrasubstituted allenes.
This approach, the first of ball-milling-based remote radical
coupling, overcomes the limitations of traditional solution-phase
methods, such as the need for air- and moisture-sensitive reagents,
the use of bulk solvents, and prolonged reaction times. Given the
outstanding performance of ball-milling-based radical reduction
coupling reactions, we anticipate further advancements in
sustainable and efficient synthetic methodologies.
M
echanochemistry, which involves the direct absorption
and utilization of mechanical energy to drive chemical
reactions, has emerged as a powerful strategy in material
science,
1
polymer chemistry,
2
and both inorganic and organic
synthesis.
3
Its primary advantages include simplicity of
operation, significant reduction in reaction times, elimination
of the extensive use of harmful organic solvents, and precise
energy control. This method is particularly suitable for
substrates with poor solubility and allows for air- and
moisture-sensitive reactions to be conducted under ambient
conditions. Ball-milling conditions can be applied to a wide
range of applications, including Buchwald−Hartwig,

3b,12
These methods often
achieve better reaction efficiency compared to traditional
solution-phase reactions, presenting exciting possibilities for
exploring previously uncharted areas of chemical space.
Allenes, which are cumulative dienes, have garnered notable
attention in pharmaceutical science and synthetic chemistry
due to their distinct biological activity and chemical
reactivity.
13
However, classic methods for allene synthesis
typically suffer from several limitations: they involve labor-
intensive steps for preparing activated substrates and require
stringent reaction conditions, especially for synthesizing
multisubstituted allenes.
14
In this context, the 1,4-functional-
ization of readily accessible 1,3-enynes offers an efficient and
practical synthetic approach for producing multisubstituted
allenes. Although the dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes
can directly form two C−C bonds to obtain multisubstituted
allenes, the polar approach via allenyl anion species usually
requires organolithium or organozinc reagents, which are
constrained by functional group compatibility and necessitate
cryogenic cooling (Figure 1A).
15
In contrast, the radical
approach has made significant progress in the 1,4-dicarbo-
functionalization of 1,3-enynes by combining single-electron
transfer processes with transition-metal catalysis.
16
Recent
advancements in the dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes
have employed not only nickel catalysis but also photo-

17
Despite these
advancements, traditional solution-phase reactions still face
challenges such as sensitivity to air and moisture, long reaction
durations, the need for large amounts of solvents, and a limited
range of coupling partners (typically relying on alkyl iodides as
radical donors). With the growing importance of sustainability
in both societal and industrial processes, there is an increasing
need to reduce the introduction of excessive harmful organic
waste, such as solvents and chemical stoichiometric waste,
while achieving efficient, widely applicable, and stable trans-
formations. In this context, our previous work has demon-
strated that nickel-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling reactions
can be successfully performed using mechanochemistry.
18
Herein, we present the first example of 1,4-alkylarylation of
1,3-enynes by combining nickel catalysis with mechanical
synthesis, which is also the first case of ball-milling-based
remote radical coupling (Figure 1C). The high vibration
frequency (30 Hz, MM500) is crucial for achieving efficient
transformation, emphasizing the importance of mechanical
grinding in effectively dispersing substrates, reagents, and
catalysts. Notably, this process does not require inert gas or dry
organic solvents, and the entire procedure can be conducted in
air without special precautions or techniques.
19
This discovery
broadens the substrate scope to include commercially available
alkyl and aryl bromides, yielding 1,4-arylalkylated products
with good functional group compatibility.
All mechanochemical reactions were conducted in a Retsch
MM500 mill (stainless-steel milling jar; 30 Hz; stainless-steel
balls). As a proof of concept, we initiated the exploration of the
reaction using 1,3-enyne (1a) and selected commercially
available 4-bromobenzonitrile (2a) and tert-butyl bromide
(3a) as model substrates. These were added, along with other
additives, to a 1.5 mL stainless-steel milling jar containing one
grinding ball (stainless, diameter: 5.0 mm) inside a glovebox.
Following simple filtration and NMR analysis, the reaction
conditions yielded tetrasubstituted allene 4a in 70%

Neither increasing the amount of LAG nor extending the
reaction time significantly enhanced the isolated yield of allene
4a (entries 13, 14), but adjusting both conditions simulta-

15). In contrast, solution-based reactions (entries 16, 17) did
not produce the desired products. Increasing the temperature
from room temperature to 50 °C under the solution conditions
of entry 17 only resulted in a 33% yield (entry 18). This
further highlights the superiority of our mechanochemical
approach for achieving efficient and practical conversion.
With the optimized reaction conditions established, we
initially explored the scopes for the 1,4-alkylarylation reaction
(Figure 2). For the alkene C2-aryl substituent, aryls with
electron-donating, electron-neutral, and electron-withdrawing
groups exhibited excellent tolerance to the reductive 1,4-
alkylarylation reaction, yielding the corresponding tetrasub-
stituted allene (4a−4j). The yields ranged from good to
excellent (64−93%), regardless of the electronic nature of the
aryl substituents of the substrate 1. As described in the
literature,
17a
this result indicates that it involves a radical
intermediate rather than anionic or cationic ones. This finding,
which indicates that the reaction is relatively insensitive to
substituent electronic effects, provides important insights for
the reaction mechanism and brings greater flexibility and
broader applicability in different conditions. Remarkably,
polyaromatic substrates, often deemed challenging substrates
in solution-based conditions due to their limited solubility,
efficiently formed the desired products (4h and 4i) in 87% and
81% yield, respectively. This provides further confirmation of
the advantages that the ball-milling reaction holds over the
traditional solution reaction. When the linear alkane on R

alkyl bromides with both acyclic and cyclic alkyl groups were
applicable to the reaction. Both acyclic and cyclic alkyl
bromides provided the products in excellent yields (6a−6d,
80−94%). Unfortunately, secondary and primary alkyl
bromides were unable to yield the corresponding allene
products (Figure S3), and TLC indicated that most of the
enyne and aryl bromides remained unreacted. This implies that
it is difficult to generate the corresponding primary alkyl and
secondary alkyl radicals under this ball-milling conditions.
18,20
To further demonstrate the practicality of our method, we
performed a gram-scale synthesis of compound 4a under
ambient air conditions, using bench-grade tetrahydrofuran as
the LAG. This process yielded 1.65 g of compound 4a, with a
yield comparable to that of the previous small-scale synthesis
(85%, Figure 3). Subsequently, a series of late-stage
functionalizations were performed on 4a to emphasize the
potential utility of the newly developed allenes. Treating allene
4a under acidic conditions generated multisubstituted 1H-
indene 7a with a 65% yield. Under alkaline conditions, the
hydration reaction of the cyano group proceeded smoothly,
yielding allyl amide 7b with a 58% yield. Additionally, using
copper chloride and di(phenylphosphino)benzene as catalysts,
allene 4a was easily converted into vinyl-Bpin 7c.
To gain a deeper understanding of the reductive 1,4-
alkylarylation pathway, a series of mechanistic experiments
were conducted (Figure 4). When 1.5 equivalents of (2,2,6,6-
tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl (TEMPO) was added (Figure
4A), the 1,4-alkylarylation of 1a was completely inhibited, and
most of the enyne and aryl bromides remained unreacted.
These results unequivocally suggested the involvement of alkyl
radicals in the reaction. To further elucidate the nickel catalytic
cycle, the aryl-nickel (II) complex Ni-1 was presynthesized and
then reacted with 1a and 3a (Figure 4B). In this scenario, the
desired product 4a was obtained with an isolated yield of 17%.
Furthermore, using Ni-1 (10 mol %) as the catalyst resulted in
a 71% yield of 4a. We attribute this to the instability of aryl-
nickel(II) complex Ni-1, which is prone to rapid decom-
position during the reaction.
21
Additionally, the use of an
equivalent amount of Ni-1 was proposed to accelerate the
formation of protonated products or direct coupling with alkyl
radicals, which ultimately decreases the yield of the desired
target compound.
22
However, when catalytic amounts of Ni-1
are used in combination with reductants and aryl bromides,
Ni-1 can be continuously regenerated. Aryl bromides are
essential for participating in the catalytic cycle, facilitating the
ongoing generation of Ni-1.
21,22

In summary, we have developed an efficient mechanochem-
ical nickel-catalyzed three-component reductive 1,4-alkylaryla-
tion method for the catalytic conversion of 1,3-enynes to
tetrasubstituted allenes. This method effectively addresses the
challenge of selectively transforming conjugated systems, such
as 1,3-enynes, which contain multiple active sites suitable for
coupling reactions. Several key advantages make this method
particularly attractive and practical. 1. Use of stable, readily
available starting materials: The reaction employs stable,
unactivated 1,3-enynes, commercially available aryl bromides,
and alkyl bromides as starting materials, avoiding the need for
air-sensitive or laboriously prepared reagents. This enhances
both the accessibility and scalability of the reaction. 2.
Simplified reaction conditions: The procedure does not require
inert conditions or high temperatures, which are often essential
for traditional reductive coupling reactions. This simplification
reduces the overall cost and complexity of the reaction setup,
making it more accessible to a wider range of chemists. 3.
Rapid and efficient transformation: Under ball-milling
conditions, various substrates can achieve rapid and efficient
transformation within a remarkably short reaction time of just
1 h, representing a significant improvement over traditional
reactions. Overall, this innovative mechanochemical approach
offers a more efficient and practical method for radical
reductive coupling reactions, with significant potential for
diverse applications in organic synthesis.
